The edge, and the pressure

botiss edge

  • Widest single-vendor range: xeno, allograft, synthetic, membranes, soft tissue, custom blocks, magnesium fixation.
  • +HyA sticky-graft handling and NOVAMag magnesium are genuinely modern differentiators.
  • maxgraft human allograft — a whole category Geistlich does not field.
  • Straumann backing: ecosystem bundle plus distribution across Europe and the Americas.

Pressure points

  • Geistlich's evidence and brand pull keep Bio-Oss the default specification.
  • Korean and EU value players compress xenograft and membrane pricing, often implant-bundled.
  • Bio-Gide leads resorbable membranes; Cytoplast leads non-resorbable.
  • The US market was cautious in 2025, and FDA or Health Canada pathways slow new formats.
Commercial desk

Your competitive intelligence, on call

Positioning, objections, pricing and account strategy. In the working version it answers your own questions from the briefing plus everything the team has logged, writes new intel back for everyone, and hands evidence questions to the science desk below. It runs on each person's own Claude account.

The exchange below was written by hand to show the shape of it. It is an illustration, not a recorded answer — a file like this cannot reach Claude. The two grey lines are the agent using its tools: reading the stored profiles, and writing a new price into the team's pool mid-conversation.
A perio in Munich says “we always use Bio-Oss, why would I switch?” What do I say?
pulled the Geistlich Pharma profile
Don't fight the evidence base, move the ground to handling and range. Bio-Oss has ~30 years of data and you will not win that argument in the chair. • Concede the point once, then reframe: "Bio-Oss is the reference, and cerabone is a phase-pure sintered HA with the same volume stability at materially better value per case." • Demonstrate +HyA. Sticky-graft handling is something they can feel chairside in two minutes; base Bio-Oss has no equivalent. • Ask what they do when they need human allograft. Geistlich has no answer there — maxgraft means they stop running two suppliers. • Price the whole case, not the granule: graft plus membrane plus fixation. Their Bio-Oss plus Bio-Gide basket is where the gap shows. • If they do complex reconstruction, lead with bonebuilder against Yxoss: milled allograft, no titanium to remove, no second surgery.
Good. Also — Geistlich quoted 158 for the 0.5 g at Dr Weber last Thursday, cash discount included.
logged a price point: Bio-Oss 0.5 g 158
Saved to the team store as a Geistlich price point for Germany, 0.5 g at 158 EUR, sourced to your visit at Dr Weber, with the cash discount noted. That is below the Munich figure already on file, so the local floor is softer than we thought. Two things follow: • Your cerabone cost-per-case story is still the stronger one once membrane is in the basket. • Worth flagging to the DACH team — if Geistlich is discounting for cash at practice level, other accounts will have heard the same number.
Science desk

Keep the claim defensible

The scientific counterpart to the commercial desk. It grades what you want to say, gives you the safe wording, explains the material science in plain words, and cites only references the team has actually verified.

It will not invent a citation. It cannot search the literature — no web access, no database — so it cites only what is in the team's evidence library, tells you which claim tier you are in, and drafts the request to Medical Affairs when the reference does not exist yet. “I have no reference for that” is the answer working correctly, not failing.
The exchange below was written by hand as an illustration, like the commercial one above. The evidence library it refers to starts empty and is filled by whoever has the reference list — every entry records what claim it can actually support, and whether Medical Affairs has signed it off.
Can I tell a perio that cerabone is volume-stable?
searched the evidence library for “cerabone volume stability”
Yes, as a tier 2 claim about design and mechanism. No, as a claim about what will happen in their patient. • Safe: “cerabone is sintered above 1200 °C, which gives a highly crystalline hydroxyapatite designed to resorb very slowly and hold graft volume.” That is processing plus mechanism, and it is in the technical file. • Not safe: “cerabone will keep your ridge volume.” That converts a mechanism into a patient outcome, which is tier 3 and needs a clinical study on this product. • If they push for the study: the evidence library has nothing on cerabone volume retention yet, so I cannot give you a citation and I am not going to invent one. • The honest line that keeps your credibility: “The mechanism is well characterised and I would rather send you our clinical data than paraphrase it — let me get that from Medical Affairs.” Request to send: clinical studies on cerabone reporting graft volume or dimensional change, with the endpoint (radiographic or histological), follow-up duration and patient numbers stated.
Fair. Medical Affairs sent me a paper on it — how do I get it in here?
Give me the title, first author, journal, year and the DOI or PMID, and say what it actually measured. I will file it in the evidence library and mark who verified it. One caution on what it will then support: if the endpoint was radiographic ridge width at six months, the claim it licenses is about radiographic dimensional change at six months, not about long-term volume stability in general. I will record it that narrowly, so nobody stretches it later.
Claims

What you may say, and who has to sign it off

The rubric the science desk grades against. Worth knowing cold: it is the difference between a claim that survives a clinician's follow-up question and one that costs you the account.

Tier 1 · Portfolio fact

low risk

Composition, origin, processing, dimensions, pack sizes, regulatory status.

Source of truthThe instructions for use and the technical file.
RuleState it freely, in the IFU's own words.

“cerabone is a sintered bovine hydroxyapatite processed above 1200 °C, with no organic residue.”

Tier 2 · Mechanism or preclinical

medium risk

How the material is designed to behave. Bench work, animal models, histology.

Source of truthPreclinical studies and the technical file.
RuleSay what it is designed to do, or what was seen in preclinical models. Never convert that into a patient outcome.

Say “designed to remain volume-stable”. Do not say “it will keep your ridge stable”.

Tier 3 · Clinical outcome for our product

high risk

Survival, success, volume retention or healing measured in patients, using this product.

Source of truthPublished clinical studies on this specific product. Nothing else counts.
RuleOnly with a reference from the evidence library, and Medical Affairs sign-off for anything written or repeated at scale.

If you cannot name the study, its design, the patient number and the follow-up, you do not have the claim.

Tier 4 · Better than a named competitor

highest risk

Any superiority claim against Bio-Oss, Bio-Gide, Cytoplast, Puros or any other named product.

Source of truthHead-to-head clinical evidence on that exact comparison.
RuleAssume you cannot say it. Route it to Medical Affairs and regulatory before it is said once.

Comparable handling in a head-to-head study is not superiority. “Better value per case” is a commercial claim, not a clinical one, and is safer ground.

Where the evidence actually stands

topics, not citations
Deliberately written without authors, years or numbers. Those belong in the evidence library, entered by someone who can verify them. This map tells you what kind of evidence exists in each area, so you know whether you are on firm ground before you open your mouth.

Deproteinized bovine bone mineral in sinus floor augmentation

Established

One of the largest bodies of work in the field: randomised trials, long-term cohorts, histomorphometry and multiple systematic reviews.

Safe to say

Bovine xenograft in sinus augmentation is one of the best-documented procedures in implant dentistry.

Do not say

Attributing that whole body of work to cerabone specifically. Most of it was generated on Bio-Oss.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Which sinus augmentation studies were run on cerabone itself, with what follow-up.

Volume stability: sintered versus non-sintered xenograft

Contested

The mechanism is well supported and independently reviewed (Miron 2024 in Periodontology 2000 states that sintering changes hydroxyapatite dissolution such that osteoclasts can no longer resorb it). The head-to-head clinical comparison against Bio-Oss rests largely on one radiographic study (Riachi 2012).

Safe to say

High-temperature sintering produces a more crystalline, slower-resorbing scaffold. The mechanism is characterised in independent reviews, not just our own literature.

Do not say

Repeating the “significantly less volumetric loss than Bio-Oss” line. That is tier 4, it rests on a single radiographic endpoint, and it needs sign-off before it is said once.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Whether anything beyond Riachi 2012 supports the head-to-head volume comparison, and with what endpoint.

Cortical versus cancellous allograft granules

Established

Two studies including a three-arm randomised trial (Eskow 2014; Demetter 2017) found no significant difference in ridge width or height change or in new bone percentage between cortical, cancellous and 50/50 allograft in socket preservation. More residual graft in the cortical arms.

Safe to say

Our granule variants are a handling and preference choice. The literature does not show one outperforming another in socket preservation, and we say so.

Do not say

Selling one granule type as clinically better than another. The evidence is against you, and a well-read clinician will know it.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Nothing — this one is settled. Use it to build credibility by conceding a point you do not need.

Xenograft versus autogenous bone for implant survival

Established

Systematic reviews across several indications generally find comparable implant survival, with autograft retaining advantages in specific defect types.

Safe to say

In many indications the literature does not show an implant survival penalty for xenograft against autograft.

Do not say

“As good as autograft” as a blanket statement. It is indication-dependent.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The reviews covering the indication in front of you, not augmentation in general.

Human allograft in ridge preservation and augmentation

Established

A substantial, largely North American literature on mineralised and demineralised allograft in socket and ridge work.

Safe to say

Allograft is a well-established option with a long clinical record, particularly in US practice.

Do not say

Implying equivalence between our processing and any other bank's. Processing differs and matters.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The processing and validation documentation for maxgraft, and what is published on that processing specifically.

Biphasic calcium phosphate: resorption and bone substitution

Established

Well-characterised mechanism, with resorption behaviour dependent on the HA to β-TCP ratio, plus clinical work across several ratios.

Safe to say

The HA to β-TCP ratio governs how quickly the scaffold gives way to bone; ours is formulated for a specific balance.

Do not say

Quoting resorption timelines as if they were patient-specific predictions.

Ask Medical Affairs for: What maxresorb's ratio was designed for and which clinical studies used that exact formulation.

Barrier duration versus soft-tissue integration

Contested

The central trade-off in the membrane literature, and genuinely unresolved. Cross-linking extends barrier function but is associated with slower integration and worse behaviour once exposed; several comparative integration studies on our own membranes sit in the library. The head-to-head pericardium against dermis comparison DOES exist (Bornert 2021, Clin Exp Dent Res, minipig): pericardium was statistically non-inferior to the control membrane on both resorption kinetics and barrier function, and the authors themselves say clinical evaluation is still needed.

Safe to say

There is a real trade-off between how long a barrier lasts and how the soft tissue handles it, and it is material-specific. On pericardium against dermis we have a preclinical non-inferiority result — cite it as the minipig study it is.

Do not say

“Longer barrier function is better.” It is the most common membrane overclaim and a well-read periodontist will push back. Also do not turn non-inferiority in minipigs into a clinical superiority claim, and do not move a finding from one collagen membrane onto another — cross-linking method matters.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Whether any CLINICAL barrier-duration comparison exists, since the strongest entry we hold is preclinical and its authors flag exactly that gap.

Membrane exposure and dehiscence

Established

Exposure is the practical driver of GBR failure and is reported across the literature for every membrane type. Rates depend far more on flap design, tension-free closure and case selection than on brand.

Safe to say

Exposure is the main thing that costs you a graft, and it is mostly about closure and case selection. Ask what happened in their exposed cases before recommending anything.

Do not say

Any claim that our membrane has a lower exposure rate. That is tier 4, needs head-to-head data, and the surgeon's technique dominates the outcome anyway.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Reported exposure and complication rates for each of our membranes, and whether any study reports them against a comparator.

Pericardium as a barrier membrane (Jason)

Emerging

Established surgical use, with a smaller published comparative base than porcine dermis or the category leader. Pericardium's multi-directional collagen architecture is the mechanistic argument.

Safe to say

Pericardium gives multi-directional tensile strength and a long barrier function from a native, non-cross-linked material.

Do not say

Claiming a comparable evidence base to Bio-Gide. On published volume that is not where we are, and pretending otherwise loses the room.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Every clinical publication on Jason, sorted by design, and an honest map of where the gaps against Bio-Gide sit.

Porcine dermis as a barrier membrane (collprotect)

Emerging

Native dermal matrix with an open structure argued to favour early vascularisation and wound adhesion, at a shorter barrier duration than pericardium.

Safe to say

A native dermis matrix with good wound adhesion, for cases where you want faster integration rather than the longest barrier.

Do not say

Positioning it as interchangeable with Jason. The two are an indication-matched pair and selling them as equivalent wastes the distinction.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The clinical evidence for collprotect specifically, and any data comparing it with Jason so the indication split can be stated properly.

dPTFE and intentionally exposed healing (permamem)

Established

The open-healing principle is well described and widely taught, and the material property — no bacterial penetration at high density, removal without a second flap — is characterised in vitro. But check the permamem entries before you lean on them: SEVEN of the twenty-five in the library are congress posters rather than peer-reviewed papers, including one whose own title says case series. The published clinical base is thinner than the reference count suggests.

Safe to say

Dense PTFE supports protocols where the membrane is intentionally left exposed and removed later, without primary closure. The in vitro work on bacterial adhesion and surface properties is solid.

Do not say

Quoting the poster material as published evidence, and presenting the reference count as the strength of the evidence. It still has to be removed, which is the honest cost against a resorbable option.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Which exposed-healing protocols permamem is validated for, its recommended in-situ duration, the removal-timing evidence, and whether any of the poster work has since been published in full.

Open healing with a magnesium membrane

Emerging

New and worth knowing: open wound healing in GBR with a magnesium membrane is now documented (Tabanella 2025, J Biomed Mater Res B) — a four-case series, whose own framing notes that soft-tissue healing complications for this membrane had not previously been reported. So exposed healing is no longer a dPTFE-only story, but the magnesium evidence for it is four cases.

Safe to say

There is now published documentation of open healing with the magnesium membrane. Four cases, so describe it as early experience, not as an established protocol.

Do not say

Presenting magnesium as validated for open healing, or comparing its exposure behaviour with dPTFE. Neither claim has the evidence behind it.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Any larger magnesium series with exposure and dehiscence outcomes, and whether an exposed-healing protocol is formally supported.

Magnesium membranes (NOVAMag) against collagen and titanium

Emerging

A genuinely new category with small datasets and short follow-up. Degradation behaviour and gas formation are the live scientific questions, and one published in vitro plus two-patient report addresses compatibility with our own grafts rather than efficacy.

Safe to say

Magnesium resorbs, so there is no removal surgery. It is a new category and we are open about the evidence being young — that honesty is worth more here than enthusiasm.

Do not say

Any long-term outcome claim, and any comparison with titanium mesh on dehiscence. Follow-up does not exist yet, and the audience most interested in this is the one that will read the papers.

Ask Medical Affairs for: All NOVAMag clinical data with follow-up durations, the degradation timeline, and how gas formation is characterised and managed.

Hyaluronic acid added to bone grafts

Emerging

Better than it looks, but narrow. One randomised controlled trial on cerabone plus in reconstructive peri-implantitis treatment (Rakašević 2023) found greater implant stability and vertical marginal bone gain against cerabone alone. Beyond that: in vitro osteoblast and angiogenesis work, a three-case histology report, and a retrospective maxgraft +HyA volumetric comparison the deck presents without a citation. Handling benefits are real but the figure behind them is a customer survey, not a study.

Safe to say

In reconstructive peri-implantitis treatment there is randomised evidence for the hyaluronate version over the same graft without it — name that indication when you cite it. Separately, hyaluronate makes the graft cohesive and easier to place.

Do not say

Stretching that one RCT into grafting in general, or turning the in vitro osteoblast work into bone formation in a patient. Do not quote the 78.5% easier-application figure without saying it is a survey of 156 clinicians.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The publication reference for the maxgraft +HyA volumetric comparison, so it can be cited properly, and what the +HyA evidence covers outside peri-implantitis.

Soft-tissue matrices versus autologous connective tissue graft

Contested

Reduced patient morbidity and shorter surgery are consistently reported. Equivalence of the tissue result is the contested part, and varies by indication.

Safe to say

A matrix avoids a palatal donor site, which reduces morbidity and chair time — that part is not controversial.

Do not say

Claiming equivalence to a connective tissue graft across the board.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The mucoderm evidence by indication, separating morbidity endpoints from tissue-outcome endpoints.

Resorbable magnesium fixation (NOVAMag screw, SHIELD)

Emerging

Same young category as the membrane, applied to fixation and buccal-wall reconstruction. Small datasets, short follow-up.

Safe to say

Fixation that resorbs, so no removal appointment. New category, evidence still building.

Do not say

Comparing it with titanium fixation on stability or complication rate. There is no head-to-head data to stand on.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The NOVAMag screw and SHIELD data separately from the membrane data — they are different products with different evidence.

Custom allogenic blocks versus titanium mesh

Emerging

Case series and cohorts rather than randomised comparison, on both sides of the comparison.

Safe to say

A milled allograft block avoids a removal surgery and a donor site. The comparative literature is early.

Do not say

Presenting bonebuilder as proven superior to Yxoss. Neither side has that evidence.

Ask Medical Affairs for: The bonebuilder case series, resorption behaviour, and reported complication rates.

Titanium mesh against a collagen membrane in horizontal augmentation

Established

Stop reaching for the trade-journal dehiscence figure: there is a randomised controlled trial (Atef 2020, Clin Implant Dent Relat Res) comparing a native collagen membrane with titanium mesh for horizontal augmentation of atrophic maxillary ridges. Both were viable techniques, but the authors conclude titanium mesh is more technique-sensitive, and that soft-tissue dehiscence and difficulty at second-stage removal should limit its use in that indication.

Safe to say

In horizontal maxillary augmentation there is randomised evidence that titanium mesh is more technique-sensitive, with dehiscence and removal difficulty limiting its use. That is the authors' own conclusion in a peer-reviewed RCT — use it instead of the poster and trade-journal numbers.

Do not say

Stretching it beyond horizontal maxillary augmentation, or reading it as a verdict on a specific competitor product. It compared a category with a category, not Yxoss with bonebuilder.

Ask Medical Affairs for: Nothing here. This is the best mesh comparison we hold, so the job is making sure the field knows it exists rather than quoting the 50% figure.

Playbook

How to win the conversation

Battlecards built from the landscape: how to position botiss against each rival type, plus the cross-cutting growth plays. Concrete moves, not slogans.

Against Geistlich — the main fight

01Don't try to out-legacy Bio-Oss on 30 years of evidence. Move the conversation to portfolio breadth, modern handling and total value per case.
02Lead with +HyA and cerabone plus. Hyaluronate sticky-graft handling is a tangible upgrade you can demonstrate chairside; base Bio-Oss has no equivalent.
03Sell the full stack from one supplier: cerabone, maxgraft, maxresorb plus the whole membrane, soft-tissue and custom-block range. Geistlich forces a second vendor for human allograft.
04Use maxgraft as the wedge wherever allograft is preferred, notably the US — Geistlich has no human allograft answer.
05Frame cerabone as clinically proven and volume-stable at materially better value; anchor on cost per case including membrane and fixation.
06Counter the ReOss/Yxoss custom story with maxgraft bonebuilder: a milled allograft block, no titanium to remove, no second surgery.

Against value and regional players

01Never race to the bottom on price. Compete on evidence, regulatory robustness and the soft-tissue plus custom range they cannot match.
02Anchor on cost per outcome, not cost per cc: one failed graft and redo dwarfs any material saving.
03Where implants are bundled, bring the Straumann and Neodent ecosystem to the table so the graft discount isn't the only lever in the room.
04Use botiss campus cases and webinars to show that routine-case savings aren't worth the risk on complex or aesthetic cases.

Against Envista / Osteogenics on membranes

01Where Cytoplast dPTFE is specified, put permamem head to head as the non-resorbable option inside a single botiss order — no second vendor.
02For resorbable cases, contrast Jason (long barrier, pericardium) against collprotect (native, wound-adhesive) to show indication-matched choice rather than one-size-fits-all.
03Bring NOVAMag where the clinician wants to avoid a removal surgery — a story creos and OsseoGuard cannot tell.

Cross-cutting growth plays

01Sell through the implant channel: roughly half of implant procedures need grafting. Co-sell with Straumann and Neodent to lift attach rate — model it in the Deal tab.
02Win full-arch and complex reconstruction first. Portfolio breadth and bonebuilder blocks are decisive there, and routine volume follows the relationship.
03Make botiss campus a lead engine: case library, webinars and hands-on sticky-bone workshops convert better than brochures.
04Match the material to the market's beliefs: maxresorb where animal origin is a barrier, maxgraft where allograft is the norm.
05Push the 2025 launches as proof of cadence: NOVAMag SHIELD, maxgraft +HyA and the seven-product white-label line.

Resorbable collagen membraneJason membrane (porcine pericardium) · collprotect (porcine dermis)Both native, neither chemically cross-linked. Jason is pericardium: multi-directional collagen architecture, so tensile strength in every direction and a longer barrier function. collprotect is dermis: an open structure argued to favour early vascularisation and wound adhesion, at a shorter barrier duration. They are an indication-matched pair, not two versions of the same thing. Markets

What drives the decision, region by region

Material preference, who is entrenched, regulatory friction and the angle that works locally.

DACH (DE · AT · CH)

Home turf · premium

Straumann distributes botiss directly and the brand is well established. Geistlich is strong on its Swiss home market. Allograft is accepted, and maxgraft is processed in Austria. Defend share; push +HyA, NOVAMag and custom blocks as the premium innovation edge.

Rest of Europe

Fragmented · MDR friction

OsteoBiol is strong in Italy and France. EU MDR raises the regulatory bar, which favours well-documented, well-funded suppliers. Reimbursement varies by country and implant work is largely private-pay. Win with the full soft-tissue range and indication-matched membranes against single-line rivals.

North America (US · CA)

Allograft-led · soft demand

An allograft-preferring culture makes maxgraft a real differentiator against Geistlich. But BioHorizons, ZimVie and Envista are entrenched and FDA pathways add friction. Straumann reported a cautious US market in 2025 with out-of-pocket treatment under pressure. Enter on the Straumann channel plus the allograft story; Canadian approvals can lag.

Latin America (Brazil-led)

Price-sensitive · ecosystem play

botiss launched via Straumann, and Neodent is huge in Brazil — bundle grafts with implants. Geistlich is strong and bought Bionnovation for local manufacturing plus a value tier. Compete on the ecosystem bundle and education rather than raw price. LATAM was a strong Straumann growth region in 2025.

APAC

Value-dominant · high volume

Korea sets aggressive value pricing and bundles with the world's highest implant volumes. Japan is conservative with strict regulation — slow to enter, premium-friendly once in. China is large and growing with strong local players, and Straumann's Shanghai campus localises supply. Lead with evidence and Straumann backing; avoid a price war.

Middle East & Africa

Synthetic-friendly · premium private

Religious and cultural concerns can disfavour porcine and sometimes bovine origin, so lead with maxresorb and educate on cerabone's high-temperature processing. Gulf private clinics are premium and brand-receptive; distribution is partner-led.

Deal maths

Price the attach rate, not the granule

About half of implant procedures need grafting, yet many accounts graft far less. This is the number that moves a conversation away from cost per cc.

Worked on these assumptions

example account

In the working version these are four fields and the figures above rewrite themselves as you type, in front of the customer. Revenue per case means graft plus membrane plus soft tissue plus fixation you would realistically supply, in your own currency.

Use this against a price objection: a clinician haggling over a few euros per cc is usually leaving far more on the table by under-grafting. Attach rate and full-case supply grow the account; discounting the graft does not.

Tell us what to change

Worth commenting on

  • Which section would you actually open in front of a customer?
  • What is missing from the battlecards, or plain wrong in them?

  • What would you ask the agent first?

How to send it

Just reply to the email this came in, quoting the section name. Blunt is more useful than polite: wrong figures, missing rivals, sections you would never open, wording that would embarrass you in front of a clinician.

Method

Where this comes from, and what it cannot do

A briefing aid assembled from public sources in June 2026. Verify anything client-facing against the primary source before it leaves your mouth.

How the working version differs from this file

  • The agent answers live, on each person's own Claude account — the first question asks their permission, and it counts against their own usage rather than a shared key.
  • Intel is one shared live pool: a price logged in Milan is on a phone in Munich immediately.
  • It runs at a web address, so an update reaches everyone at once with nothing to reinstall.
  • It needs a Claude sign-in and organisation membership, which is exactly why this review copy exists instead.

Limits worth stating out loud

  • Market sizes differ between analysts because the definitions differ — graft-only against graft plus membranes plus soft tissue. Ranges beat false precision.
  • Share splits here are synthesised estimates, not published figures. Brief with them; never quote them to a customer.
  • Prices are quote-based. The anchors above are grey-market orientation, not channel prices.
  • Every price, note and learning shown in this file is invented example data.
  • Nothing here is clinical, regulatory, legal or financial advice, and the agent can be wrong. Check before it reaches a clinician.
